questions.q: Who gave the wealth definition of economics?
questions.why: Adam Smith, in 1776, described economics as the science of wealth: how nations produce and grow wealth.

questions.q: Marshall's definition of economics puts the main stress on:
questions.why: Marshall said economics studies how people earn and use income to gain material welfare; wealth is only a means.

questions.q: Robbins called economics the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have:
questions.why: Because scarce means can be used in more than one way, people must choose among their wants.

questions.q: The study of how one firm fixes the price of its product belongs to:
questions.why: Microeconomics studies individual units such as a consumer, a firm or one market.

questions.q: Adam Smith's famous book, published in 1776, is:
o: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science
questions.why: The Wealth of Nations (1776) is Smith's work; Principles of Economics is Marshall's and the Essay is Robbins'.

long.q: State the wealth definition of economics and give two criticisms of it.
scheme: B1: Adam Smith defined economics as the science of wealth, studying how wealth is produced and increased
B1: criticism: it gives wealth first place and treats man as secondary
B1: criticism: it takes too narrow a meaning of wealth (material goods only) and ignores welfare and services

long.q: Explain Robbins' scarcity definition of economics by stating its three main ideas.
scheme: B1: human wants (ends) are unlimited
B1: the means (resources) to satisfy them are scarce
B1: scarce means have alternative uses, so people must choose which wants to satisfy first

long.q: Distinguish between microeconomics and macroeconomics, with one example of each.
scheme: B1: microeconomics studies individual units, e.g. the demand of one household or the price of one good
B1: macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, e.g. national income, total employment or the general price level

long.q: Give two ways in which Marshall's welfare definition improved on Smith's wealth definition.
scheme: B1: it puts human welfare first and treats wealth only as a means to welfare
B1: it makes economics a social science that studies ordinary people in the ordinary business of life

long.q: Give the growth-oriented definition of economics associated with Samuelson. Why is it considered more dynamic than Robbins' definition?
scheme: B1: economics studies how people and society choose to use scarce resources with alternative uses to produce goods over time and distribute them for consumption, now and in the future
B1: it adds the element of time: how resources can be increased and used for growth
B1: Robbins' definition looks only at allocating given resources at a point of time, so it is static

questions.q: The air we breathe in the open is an example of:
questions.why: A free good is a gift of nature available in plenty, so it has no price.

questions.q: A tractor used by a farmer for ploughing is:
questions.why: It is used to produce other goods (crops), so it is a producer or capital good.

questions.q: The want-satisfying power of a commodity is called:
questions.why: Utility is the capacity of a good or service to satisfy a human want.

questions.q: Which is a characteristic of human wants?
o: They do not compete with each other
questions.why: Wants are endless, and many, such as hunger, come back again and again.

questions.q: Which economic entity buys goods for final consumption and supplies the factors of production?
questions.why: Households consume goods and services and supply land, labour, capital and enterprise to firms.

long.q: Name four economic entities in an economy and state the role of any two.
scheme: B1: households (consumers), firms (producers), government and the rest of the world
B1: role of one, e.g. firms hire factors of production and produce goods and services
B1: role of another, e.g. the government collects taxes and provides public services such as roads and defence

long.q: Distinguish between free goods and economic goods, with an example of each.
scheme: B1: free goods are available in plenty, have no price and need no effort to obtain, e.g. sunlight
B1: economic goods are scarce, have a price and need resources to produce, e.g. a bicycle

long.q: Classify each of these goods: (a) bread bought by a family (b) wheat flour bought by a bakery (c) a sewing machine used by a tailor (d) a car bought for family use.
scheme: B1: (a) consumer good (single-use / non-durable, final good)
B1: (b) intermediate good (used up in producing bread)
B1: (c) producer (capital) good
B1: (d) consumer durable good

long.q: Explain value in use and value in exchange, using the example of water and diamonds.
scheme: B1: value in use is the utility of a good; value in exchange is the amount of other goods or money it can be exchanged for
B1: water has a very high value in use but a low value in exchange because it is plentiful
B1: diamonds have little value in use but a very high value in exchange because they are scarce

long.q: State three features of services that distinguish them from goods.
scheme: B1: services are intangible: they cannot be seen or touched
B1: they are produced and consumed at the same time (inseparable from the provider)
B1: they cannot be stored for later use (perishable); they also vary from one occasion to another

questions.q: In a capitalist economy, the central problems are solved mainly by:
questions.why: Demand and supply in free markets decide what, how and for whom to produce.

questions.q: Which is a feature of a socialist economy?
o: Private ownership of most means of production
State (collective) ownership of the means of production
questions.why: In socialism the state owns the main means of production and plans production for social welfare.

questions.q: India is an example of:
questions.why: In India the public and private sectors work side by side, with government planning and regulation.

questions.q: Consumer sovereignty is mainly a feature of:
questions.why: In capitalism producers make what consumers demand, so consumers are said to be 'king'.

questions.q: Which is typical of a developing economy?
o: A very high per capita income
A large share of the workforce in agriculture
questions.why: Developing economies such as India still have a large part of the workforce depending on agriculture.

long.q: State four features of a capitalist economy.
scheme: B1: private ownership of property and the means of production
B1: profit motive guides production
B1: the price mechanism solves the central problems; there is little government interference
B1: competition among producers, and consumer sovereignty

long.q: Give two merits and two demerits of a socialist economy.
scheme: B1: merit: income and wealth are more equally distributed
B1: merit: planning allows resources to be used for social welfare, with less unemployment
B1: demerit: there is little incentive to work hard or take risks, so efficiency is low
B1: demerit: consumers have little freedom of choice and there can be excessive bureaucracy

long.q: Why is India called a mixed economy? Give two reasons.
scheme: B1: public sector enterprises (e.g. Indian Railways) and private firms exist side by side
B1: markets work freely in many areas, but the government plans, regulates and runs welfare programmes

long.q: Distinguish between a developed and a developing economy on three bases.
scheme: B1: per capita income: high in a developed economy, low in a developing one
B1: occupation: most people work in industry and services in a developed economy, in agriculture in a developing one
B1: standard of living and infrastructure (health, education, technology) are much better in a developed economy

long.q: Explain how the price mechanism works in a capitalist economy.
scheme: B1: prices are fixed by the free interaction of demand and supply
B1: when demand for a good rises its price rises, so producers find it profitable to make more of it
B1: prices of factors decide how goods are produced and incomes decide for whom; no central authority is needed

questions.q: The root cause of all economic problems is:
o: Scarcity of resources compared with wants
questions.why: Because resources are scarce compared with unlimited wants, every economy must make choices.

questions.q: Choosing between labour-intensive and capital-intensive methods is the problem of:
questions.why: 'How to produce' concerns the choice of technique, i.e. which combination of factors to use.

questions.q: The problem 'for whom to produce' concerns:
o: How output and income are shared among people
questions.why: It is the problem of distributing the national product among the people of the economy.

questions.q: A resource is said to have alternative uses when:
o: It can be used for only one purpose
It can be put to more than one use
questions.why: For example, a piece of land can grow rice or wheat, or hold a factory.

questions.q: Opportunity cost is:
o: The money spent on a good
The value of the next best alternative given up
questions.why: When a resource is used one way, the best other use given up is its opportunity cost.

long.q: Explain the three central problems of an economy.
scheme: B1: what to produce and how much: which goods (e.g. food or weapons, consumer or capital goods) and in what quantities
B1: how to produce: which technique to use, labour-intensive or capital-intensive
B1: for whom to produce: how the output is distributed among the people

long.q: Why does the problem of choice arise? Give two reasons.
scheme: B1: human wants are unlimited, while the resources to satisfy them are scarce
B1: resources have alternative uses, so using them for one want means giving up another

long.q: A farmer in Punjab can grow either wheat or sugarcane on his land. Use this to explain scarcity, choice and opportunity cost.
scheme: B1: scarcity: the land is limited and cannot grow all the crops he would like
B1: choice: he must decide which crop to grow, e.g. wheat
B1: opportunity cost: the sugarcane he could have grown is the cost of choosing wheat

long.q: Classify resources into natural, human and capital resources, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: natural resources: gifts of nature, e.g. land, water, minerals
B1: human resources: people's physical and mental abilities, e.g. labour and skills
B1: capital resources: man-made aids to production, e.g. machines, tools, buildings

long.q: Explain how a capitalist economy and a socialist economy solve the problem of 'what to produce'.
scheme: B1: capitalist: producers make the goods that consumers demand and that earn the most profit (price mechanism)
B1: socialist: a central planning authority decides what to produce according to social needs and priorities

topics.name: Main sectors of the Indian economy

questions.q: Fishing belongs to the:
questions.why: The primary sector uses natural resources directly: farming, fishing, forestry and mining.

questions.q: Which sector contributes the largest share of India's GDP today?
questions.why: Services such as trade, transport, banking and IT now produce more than half of India's output.

questions.q: A sugar mill turning sugarcane into sugar is part of the:
questions.why: The secondary sector processes raw materials into finished goods by manufacturing.

questions.q: Which sector still employs the largest share of India's workers?
questions.why: Although its share of output has fallen, agriculture remains the largest employer in India.

questions.q: Indian Railways is an example of an enterprise in the:
questions.why: It is owned and run by the Government of India, so it belongs to the public sector.

long.q: Explain the interdependence of the three sectors with the example of cotton.
scheme: B1: primary: farmers grow cotton
B1: secondary: textile mills use the cotton to make cloth, and also supply machines and fertilisers to farmers
B1: tertiary: transport, banks, warehouses and shops move, finance and sell the cotton and the cloth

long.q: Distinguish between the organised and the unorganised sectors (three points).
scheme: B1: organised enterprises are registered with the government and follow its rules; unorganised ones are mostly small and unregistered
B1: organised-sector jobs are regular, with fixed hours and paid leave; unorganised jobs are irregular and low-paid
B1: organised workers get job security and benefits such as provident fund; unorganised workers have little security

long.q: Name the sector to which each belongs: (a) mining coal (b) a bank (c) a car factory (d) a teacher.
scheme: B1: (a) primary, (c) secondary
B1: (b) and (d) tertiary

long.q: Distinguish between the public sector and the private sector, giving one Indian example of each.
scheme: B1: ownership: the public sector is owned by the government; the private sector by individuals or companies
B1: motive: the public sector aims at public welfare; the private sector mainly at profit
B1: public-sector example, e.g. Indian Railways or State Bank of India
B1: private-sector example, e.g. Tata Steel or Reliance Industries

long.q: Give three reasons why the share of the tertiary sector in India's economy is growing.
scheme: B1: as incomes rise, people demand more services such as tourism, restaurants and private schools
B1: the growth of agriculture and industry needs more transport, storage, banking and trade
B1: new information and communication technology services (software, call centres) have grown rapidly

questions.q: The Green Revolution of the late 1960s mainly increased India's output of:
questions.why: High-yielding varieties of wheat, with irrigation and fertilisers, raised output sharply, especially in Punjab and Haryana.

questions.q: Sub-division and fragmentation of land holdings lead to:
questions.why: Dividing land among heirs leaves tiny scattered plots on which machines and irrigation are hard to use.

questions.q: The government announces a Minimum Support Price to:
o: Fix the retail price of all goods
Guarantee farmers a minimum price for their crop
questions.why: If market prices fall below the MSP, the government buys the crop at the MSP, protecting farmers' incomes.

questions.q: Excessive use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides leads to:
questions.why: Chemicals harm soil organisms, wash into rivers and groundwater, and reduce fertility over time.

questions.q: Agriculture supports industry by providing:
o: Raw materials such as cotton, jute and sugarcane
questions.why: Agro-based industries such as textiles and sugar depend on farm produce.

long.q: State four ways in which agriculture contributes to the Indian economy.
scheme: B1: it provides food for the population and fodder for animals
B1: it employs the largest share of India's workforce
B1: it supplies raw materials to agro-based industries
B1: it earns foreign exchange through exports (e.g. tea, rice, spices) and provides a market for industrial goods

long.q: Explain three problems of Indian agriculture.
scheme: B1: small and fragmented holdings make modern methods uneconomic
B1: dependence on the monsoon, as a large part of farmland lacks assured irrigation
B1: lack of cheap credit and poor marketing, so farmers depend on moneylenders and middlemen (also accept outdated techniques or soil degradation)

long.q: Suggest three measures to raise agricultural productivity in India.
scheme: B1: expand irrigation, e.g. canals, tube wells and drip irrigation
B1: supply good-quality seeds, balanced fertilisers and modern tools
B1: provide cheap institutional credit (e.g. Kisan Credit Cards), crop insurance and better market facilities

long.q: Explain two harmful effects of modern farming practices on the ecosystem and suggest one remedy.
scheme: B1: over-use of fertilisers and pesticides damages soil and pollutes water bodies
B1: excessive pumping of groundwater for irrigation lowers the water table (also accept loss of biodiversity or soil salinity)
B1: remedy, e.g. organic farming, crop rotation, integrated pest management or drip irrigation

long.q: Why is Indian agriculture often described as a 'gamble in the monsoon'?
scheme: B1: much of India's farmland depends on monsoon rain because it lacks assured irrigation
B1: a late, weak or excessive monsoon causes drought or floods, so crop output varies greatly from year to year

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason for rapid industrialisation in India?
questions.why: Industrialisation reduces, not increases, the economy's dependence on rain-fed farming.

questions.q: Agriculture helps industry by providing:
o: Raw materials and a market for industrial goods
questions.why: Farms supply raw materials to industry, and farmers buy industrial goods such as tools, fertilisers and clothes.

questions.q: The Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984 was caused by a leak of:
questions.why: Methyl isocyanate gas leaked from a pesticide plant, killing thousands of people.

questions.q: An effluent treatment plant in a factory reduces:
questions.why: It treats waste water to remove harmful chemicals before it is released into rivers.

questions.q: Handloom weaving done at home with family members' labour is:
questions.why: Cottage industries are run at home by a family, with little capital and simple tools.

long.q: Explain the need for rapid industrialisation in India (four points).
scheme: B1: it creates jobs for the growing workforce and reduces pressure on land
B1: it raises national income and per capita income
B1: it makes the country self-reliant, reducing imports and increasing exports
B1: it modernises agriculture by supplying machines, fertilisers and processing units, and helps develop backward regions

long.q: How does industry help agriculture? Give two ways.
scheme: B1: it supplies inputs such as tractors, pumps, fertilisers and pesticides
B1: agro-processing industries buy farm produce and provide a market for it (also accept: employs surplus farm labour)

long.q: State three harmful effects of industrial activity on the ecosystem.
scheme: B1: smoke and gases from factories pollute the air and cause breathing diseases
B1: untreated waste water pollutes rivers and kills aquatic life
B1: solid and hazardous waste pollutes land, and forests are cleared for industries and mining

long.q: Suggest three measures to control industrial pollution.
scheme: B1: factories should install filters, scrubbers and effluent treatment plants
B1: industries should be located away from residential areas, with green belts around them
B1: strict enforcement of pollution-control laws and use of cleaner fuels and technology

long.q: Distinguish between small-scale and large-scale industries (three points).
scheme: B1: capital: small-scale industries use little capital; large-scale ones need huge investment
B1: technique: small-scale industries are labour-intensive; large-scale ones are capital-intensive with heavy machinery
B1: output and market: small-scale units produce small amounts for local markets; large-scale units produce in bulk for national and world markets

questions.q: Which of these is a tertiary activity?
questions.why: Transport is a service that helps other sectors; it produces no tangible good itself.

questions.q: Which mode is generally cheapest for carrying bulky goods such as coal over long distances by land?
questions.why: Trains carry very large loads at a low cost per tonne-kilometre over long distances.

questions.q: IT-enabled services such as call centres belong to the:
questions.why: They provide services, not goods, so they are part of the tertiary sector.

questions.q: Services differ from goods because services are:
questions.why: A haircut or a bus ride cannot be touched or kept for later use.

questions.q: Pipelines are mainly used to transport:
questions.why: Pipelines move liquids and gases cheaply and continuously over long distances.

long.q: Explain three ways in which the tertiary sector supports the primary and secondary sectors.
scheme: B1: transport carries raw materials to factories and finished goods to markets
B1: banks provide loans to farmers and industrialists
B1: storage, trade and communication help goods reach buyers and producers obtain information (also accept insurance)

long.q: State four advantages of road transport in India.
scheme: B1: it provides door-to-door service
B1: it is cheaper and quicker for short distances
B1: it reaches villages, hills and remote areas where railways do not go
B1: it is flexible in routes and timing and suits perishable goods such as milk and vegetables

long.q: Explain the importance of the services sector for employment and for regional development.
scheme: B1: it is the fastest-growing source of jobs, in trade, transport, education, health, banking and IT
B1: services such as schools, hospitals and banks in backward areas raise living standards there
B1: good transport and communication link backward regions to markets and attract industries, reducing regional imbalance

long.q: Distinguish between rail transport and road transport (two points).
scheme: B1: railways are cheaper for bulky goods over long distances; roads are cheaper for short distances
B1: railways run only on fixed tracks and timetables; roads give door-to-door service with flexible routes

long.q: Name two social services and two economic services provided in the tertiary sector.
scheme: B1: social services, e.g. education and health care
B1: economic services, e.g. banking and transport (or insurance, trade, communication)

questions.q: India's poverty line was traditionally based on a minimum daily calorie intake per person of about:
questions.why: Rural people were taken to need more calories (2400) because their work is more physically demanding than urban work (2100).

questions.q: Under MGNREGA, each rural household is guaranteed wage employment for up to how many days a year?
questions.why: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 guarantees 100 days of unskilled manual work a year.

questions.q: Poverty judged by comparing a person's income with that of others in society is:
questions.why: Relative poverty measures how poor a person is compared with others, not against a fixed minimum.

questions.q: Which is a cause of poverty in India?
questions.why: A fast-growing population lowers per capita income and puts pressure on jobs, land and services.

questions.q: The National Food Security Act was passed in:
questions.why: The 2013 Act gives a legal right to subsidised food grains to a large part of the population through the PDS.

long.q: What is a poverty line? How has it been fixed in India?
scheme: B1: the poverty line is a minimum level of income or spending needed to meet basic needs; people below it are counted as poor
B1: it has been based on the money needed for a minimum calorie intake (2400 kcal rural, 2100 kcal urban), and later on spending on food and other basic needs such as health and education

long.q: Explain four causes of poverty in India.
scheme: B1: rapid population growth, which reduces per capita income
B1: unemployment and underemployment, especially in rural areas
B1: low productivity of agriculture, on which most of the poor depend
B1: unequal distribution of income and assets such as land (also accept illiteracy or rising prices)

long.q: Distinguish between absolute poverty and relative poverty.
scheme: B1: absolute poverty: income too low to buy the minimum basic needs (food, clothing, shelter), measured by a poverty line
B1: relative poverty: income low compared with others in society; it shows inequality and exists even in rich countries

long.q: Describe two government programmes in India for reducing poverty.
scheme: B1: MGNREGA (2005)
B1: guarantees 100 days of wage employment a year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer for unskilled work
B1: a second programme, e.g. the Public Distribution System under the National Food Security Act, 2013 (or Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana)
B1: a correct feature, e.g. subsidised or free food grains through ration shops (or help to build pucca houses for the poor)

long.q: Explain how poverty and unemployment form a vicious circle.
scheme: B1: unemployed people have little or no income, so they are poor
B1: poor families cannot afford good food, health care or education, so their skills and productivity stay low
B1: low skills keep them unemployed or in low-paid work, so the poverty continues to the next generation

questions.q: Five family members work on a small farm where three would be enough. The extra two are:
questions.why: They appear to be working, but taking them away would not reduce output: their marginal productivity is zero.

questions.q: Farm workers who find no work after the harvest is over face:
questions.why: Seasonal unemployment occurs in the months of the year when there is no farm work.

questions.q: Unemployment caused by a mismatch between workers' skills and the jobs available, after changes in technology, is:
questions.why: When the structure of the economy changes, old skills are no longer in demand.

questions.q: A person between two jobs, while searching for a better one, is:
questions.why: Frictional unemployment is short-term and arises while people move between jobs.

questions.q: The Skill India Mission (2015) mainly aims to:
o: Train young people in job-related skills
questions.why: Better skills make young people employable and reduce structural and educated unemployment.

long.q: Explain disguised unemployment. Why is it hard to identify?
scheme: B1: more people are engaged in a job than are needed, so the extra workers add nothing to output (zero marginal productivity), as on small family farms
B1: it is hidden because all the workers appear to be employed and share the work and income

long.q: State four causes of unemployment in India.
scheme: B1: rapid population growth adds more people to the labour force than jobs are created
B1: slow growth of industry and over-dependence on agriculture
B1: an education system that gives little vocational or job-related training
B1: use of capital-intensive techniques and lack of capital for self-employment

long.q: Distinguish between seasonal unemployment and structural unemployment.
scheme: B1: seasonal: people lack work during certain months of the year, e.g. farm labour after the harvest
B1: structural: long-term unemployment caused by changes in the economy's structure or technology, so workers' skills no longer match the jobs

long.q: Explain three measures taken by the government to reduce unemployment.
scheme: B1: MGNREGA provides wage employment in rural areas
B1: skill-development programmes (Skill India, Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana) train youth
B1: loans and support for self-employment and small enterprises (e.g. Startup India, PMEGP, MUDRA loans)

long.q: What is educated unemployment? Give two reasons for it in India.
scheme: B1: educated unemployment exists when people with school or college education cannot find jobs suited to their qualifications
B1: the education system is largely theoretical and not linked to the skills employers need
B1: the number of graduates has grown faster than suitable jobs, and many prefer only white-collar jobs

questions.q: India introduced its New Economic Policy of liberalisation in:
questions.why: Faced with a balance of payments crisis, India began major economic reforms in July 1991.

questions.q: Selling part of the government's shares in public sector enterprises to private investors is called:
questions.why: Disinvestment reduces government ownership and is a method of privatisation.

questions.q: The World Trade Organization came into existence on 1 January 1995, replacing:
questions.why: The WTO took over from the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1947.

questions.q: Removing licences and controls on the setting up and expansion of industries is:
questions.why: Liberalisation frees the economy from government controls such as industrial licensing.

questions.q: A company that owns or controls production in more than one country is a:
questions.why: Multinational corporations (MNCs) spread production and sales across many countries.

long.q: State two objectives of India's New Economic Policy of 1991.
scheme: B1: to overcome the balance of payments crisis and control inflation
B1: to raise the rate of growth by making the economy more competitive and open to world trade and investment

long.q: Explain three measures of liberalisation taken in India after 1991.
scheme: B1: industrial licensing was abolished for most industries
B1: import duties were reduced and quantitative restrictions on imports were removed
B1: foreign direct investment was allowed in more sectors (also accept financial-sector reforms, such as the entry of private banks)

long.q: Give three arguments in favour of privatisation.
scheme: B1: private firms, driven by profit, are usually more efficient
B1: it reduces the financial burden of loss-making public enterprises on the government
B1: money from disinvestment can be used for welfare and infrastructure, and competition improves quality for consumers

long.q: State four objectives or functions of the World Trade Organization.
scheme: B1: to reduce tariffs and other barriers to international trade
B1: to set and administer rules for world trade
B1: to settle trade disputes between member countries
B1: to promote the optimum use of world resources and raise living standards, with attention to developing countries

long.q: Explain two favourable and two unfavourable effects of globalisation on India.
scheme: B1: favourable: consumers get a wider choice of better-quality goods at lower prices
B1: favourable: foreign investment and new technology flowed in, creating jobs, especially in IT services
B1: unfavourable: small producers find it hard to compete with large MNCs and imports
B1: unfavourable: many jobs became temporary or insecure, and income inequality increased

topics.name: Emerging trends in the Indian economy

questions.q: The Smart Cities Mission was launched in 2015 with the aim of developing:
questions.why: One hundred cities were selected to be developed with better infrastructure and smart solutions.

questions.q: UPI, which lets people send money instantly using a mobile phone, was developed by:
o: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI)
questions.why: NPCI launched the Unified Payments Interface in 2016.

questions.q: The Digital India programme aims mainly to:
o: Make India a digitally empowered society and knowledge economy
questions.why: It aims at digital infrastructure for every citizen, online government services and digital literacy.

questions.q: The Make in India campaign (2014) was launched to:
questions.why: It invites Indian and foreign companies to manufacture in India, creating jobs and raising output.

questions.q: Which is a feature of a smart city?
o: Efficient public transport and online public services
questions.why: Smart cities use technology to provide efficient transport, water, power and e-governance.

long.q: State four features of a smart city.
scheme: B1: assured water and electricity supply, and proper sanitation and solid-waste management
B1: efficient public transport and urban mobility
B1: robust IT connectivity and e-governance (online public services)
B1: safety of citizens, affordable housing and a sustainable, clean environment

long.q: Explain two benefits of Digital India for people living in villages.
scheme: B1: government services such as certificates, land records and benefit payments can be obtained online, without travelling to offices
B1: digital payments, online banking and information on prices, weather and farming methods help villagers and farmers

long.q: Give three reasons why India needs smart cities.
scheme: B1: rapid urbanisation has put heavy pressure on housing, water, transport and power in cities
B1: traffic congestion, pollution and slums lower the quality of urban life
B1: well-planned cities attract investment and create jobs, helping economic growth

long.q: Explain three ways in which digital payments such as UPI have changed the Indian economy.
scheme: B1: payments have become quick, cheap and possible at any time, even for small amounts
B1: more transactions are recorded, reducing the use of cash and helping to check tax evasion
B1: small shopkeepers and street vendors can accept payments easily, bringing them into the formal financial system

long.q: State three challenges in implementing Digital India.
scheme: B1: the digital divide: many rural and poor people lack smartphones or reliable Internet
B1: low digital literacy, especially among older and rural people
B1: risks of cyber fraud and threats to the privacy of personal data

questions.q: In economics, land includes:
o: Only the soil of a farm
All free gifts of nature, such as soil, water, minerals and forests
questions.why: Land means every natural resource that helps production and is not made by man.

questions.q: Which is a characteristic of land?
o: Its supply can be increased at will
It can be moved from place to place
questions.why: The total area of the earth cannot be increased, so the supply of land is fixed.

questions.q: Land is called a passive factor of production because:
o: It produces only when labour and capital work on it
questions.why: Land cannot produce anything by itself; human effort and capital must be applied to it.

questions.q: The reward paid for the use of land is:
questions.why: Rent is the reward for land, wages for labour, interest for capital and profit for the entrepreneur.

questions.q: The productivity of land depends on:
o: Its fertility, location and the improvements made on it
The number of its owners only
questions.why: Fertile, well-located land with irrigation and other improvements produces more.

long.q: State four characteristics of land.
scheme: B1: land is a free gift of nature
B1: its total supply is fixed
B1: it is geographically immobile
B1: it is a passive factor and its quality (fertility, location) differs from place to place

long.q: Explain three factors that affect the productivity of land.
scheme: B1: natural fertility of the soil, together with climate and rainfall
B1: location: land near markets, roads or cities is more productive and valuable
B1: improvements and methods of cultivation, such as irrigation, fertilisers, good seeds and machines

long.q: Land is said to be immobile. Explain how it is geographically immobile but mobile between uses.
scheme: B1: land cannot be shifted from one place to another, so it is geographically immobile
B1: the same piece of land can be used for different purposes, e.g. changed from growing rice to building houses, so it is mobile between uses

long.q: Name the four factors of production and the reward each one earns.
scheme: B1: land earns rent
B1: labour earns wages
B1: capital earns interest
B1: the entrepreneur earns profit

long.q: Plots of land differ in fertility and location. Explain, with an Indian example, how this affects the rent they earn.
scheme: B1: land is heterogeneous: no two plots are exactly alike in fertility or position
B1: example, e.g. a shop plot on a busy market road in Mumbai or a fertile irrigated field in Punjab compared with a remote or dry plot
B1: more fertile or better-located land yields more output or business, so it earns a higher rent

questions.q: Which of these is NOT labour in economics?
o: A teacher teaching for a salary
A mother cooking for her own family without payment
A worker in a cement factory
A doctor working in a hospital
questions.why: Labour is human effort done for a monetary reward; unpaid work done out of love is not counted.

questions.q: Labour is said to be perishable because:
o: A day's labour, if not used, is lost for ever
questions.why: A worker who is idle for a day cannot store that day's work for later.

questions.q: In a car factory, different groups of workers make the engine, the body and the paint finish. This is:
questions.why: The making of one product is split into several processes, each done by a different set of workers.

questions.q: The reward paid for labour is:
questions.why: Wages (or salary) are paid for physical or mental work.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of division of labour for workers?
o: Doing the same task repeatedly becomes monotonous
questions.why: Repeating one small task all day is dull and gives little satisfaction in the work.

long.q: State four characteristics of labour.
scheme: B1: labour cannot be separated from the labourer
B1: labour is perishable: it cannot be stored
B1: labour is less mobile than capital, and its supply cannot be changed quickly
B1: labour is an active factor, and individual workers have weak bargaining power

long.q: Explain three advantages of division of labour to the producer.
scheme: B1: workers become specialised and more skilled, so output and quality rise
B1: time is saved, as workers do not move from one task to another
B1: machines can be used for simple, repeated tasks, so the cost of production per unit falls

long.q: Give three reasons for the low efficiency of Indian labour.
scheme: B1: poor health and nutrition
B1: low levels of education and technical training
B1: poor working conditions and outdated machinery and methods (also accept hot climate or lack of incentives)

long.q: Distinguish between simple division of labour and complex (process) division of labour, with an example of each.
scheme: B1: simple: society divides into occupations and each person makes a whole product or does a whole job, e.g. a farmer, a carpenter, a tailor
B1: complex: the making of one product is split into processes, each done by different workers, e.g. cutting, stitching and buttoning in a garment factory

long.q: Explain territorial (geographical) division of labour with an Indian example.
scheme: B1: different regions specialise in producing particular goods for which they have advantages of raw materials, skills or climate
B1: example, e.g. diamond cutting in Surat, brassware in Moradabad or hosiery in Ludhiana

questions.q: Capital is:
o: A man-made means of further production
Only money kept in a bank
questions.why: Capital is wealth made by man and used to produce more goods, such as tools, machines and buildings.

questions.q: A machine used in a factory for many years is:
questions.why: Fixed capital is used again and again over many rounds of production.

questions.q: Raw materials that are used up in a single round of production form:
questions.why: Circulating capital, such as cotton in a mill, is used up and changes form in one use.

questions.q: Shares, bonds and bank deposits are examples of:
questions.why: They are money assets or claims that are used to obtain physical capital.

questions.q: The first step in capital formation is:
questions.why: People must first save part of their income before it can be collected and invested.

long.q: State four characteristics of capital.
scheme: B1: capital is man-made
B1: it is a passive factor: it produces only when labour works with it
B1: it is the most mobile factor of production
B1: it depreciates (wears out) with use, and its supply can be increased by saving

long.q: Distinguish between fixed capital and circulating capital.
scheme: B1: fixed capital is used many times over a long period, e.g. machines and buildings
B1: circulating capital is used up in a single use, e.g. raw materials and fuel

long.q: Explain the three stages of capital formation.
scheme: B1: creation of savings: households and firms save part of their income
B1: mobilisation of savings: banks and other financial institutions collect these savings
B1: investment: the savings are lent to producers who use them to buy machines, buildings and other capital goods

long.q: Give three reasons why capital formation is essential for a developing economy like India.
scheme: B1: it raises production and the productivity of labour, increasing national income
B1: it creates employment through new industries and infrastructure
B1: it allows the use of better technology and the development of infrastructure such as roads and power

long.q: Give two reasons for low capital formation in India and suggest one measure to raise it.
scheme: B1: low incomes mean people can save very little
B1: savings are often kept in unproductive forms such as gold, or not reached by banks in rural areas
B1: measure, e.g. spreading banking to villages and offering attractive savings schemes, or encouraging foreign investment

questions.q: The reward of an entrepreneur is:
questions.why: The entrepreneur earns profit, the reward for organising production and bearing uncertainty.

questions.q: Which risk faced by an entrepreneur cannot be insured?
o: A fall in demand for the product in future
questions.why: Uncertainty about future demand cannot be measured, so no insurance company will cover it.

questions.q: Bringing land, labour and capital together in the right proportion is called:
questions.why: The entrepreneur combines the other factors so that production is efficient.

questions.q: Introducing a new product or a new method of production is called:
questions.why: Innovation is a key function of the entrepreneur and drives economic progress.

questions.q: Entrepreneurs help balanced regional development by:
o: Setting up units only in big cities
Setting up units in backward areas
questions.why: New units in backward areas create jobs and incomes there, reducing regional inequality.

long.q: Explain four functions of an entrepreneur.
scheme: B1: initiation: having the business idea and deciding what to produce
B1: organisation: hiring and combining land, labour and capital in the right proportions
B1: risk and uncertainty bearing: accepting possible losses
B1: innovation and decision-making: introducing new products or methods and making key business decisions

long.q: Distinguish between risk and uncertainty.
scheme: B1: risks, such as fire or theft, can be foreseen and calculated, so they can be insured
B1: uncertainties, such as changes in demand or fashion, cannot be calculated, so they cannot be insured and must be borne by the entrepreneur

long.q: Explain the role of entrepreneurs in economic development (three points).
scheme: B1: they mobilise savings and invest them, raising capital formation
B1: they set up enterprises that create employment and raise national income
B1: they bring innovation and help balanced regional development and exports

long.q: Why is the entrepreneur called the 'captain of industry'?
scheme: B1: the entrepreneur leads and directs the whole business, deciding what, how and how much to produce
B1: the entrepreneur controls and coordinates the other factors and bears the final responsibility for success or failure

long.q: Name the factor of production that (a) is a free gift of nature (b) bears uncertainty (c) is man-made (d) cannot be separated from its owner.
scheme: B1: (a) land, (b) entrepreneur
B1: (c) capital, (d) labour

questions.q: In economics, demand means:
o: Desire backed by the ability and willingness to pay, at a given price and time
questions.why: A mere wish is not demand; the buyer must also be able and willing to pay a stated price.

questions.q: Other things being equal, a fall in the price of tea causes:
o: A shift of the demand curve to the right
An extension of demand (a movement down along the curve)
questions.why: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the same demand curve: here, an extension.

questions.q: Tea and coffee are:
questions.why: They can be used in place of each other, so a rise in the price of one raises demand for the other.

questions.q: A rise in consumers' income, for a normal good, causes:
o: A movement along the demand curve
A shift of the demand curve to the right (an increase in demand)
questions.why: Income is a factor other than price, so a change in it shifts the whole demand curve.

questions.q: At ₹20 a kilogram, consumer A buys 4 kg and consumer B buys 6 kg. They are the only buyers. What is the market demand at ₹20?
questions.why: Market demand is the sum of individual demands at each price: 4 + 6 = 10 kg.

long.q: State the law of demand and two of its assumptions.
scheme: B1: other things remaining the same, the quantity demanded of a good rises when its price falls and falls when its price rises (an inverse relationship)
B1: assumption: consumers' income and tastes do not change
B1: assumption: the prices of related goods (substitutes and complements) do not change

long.q: Distinguish between an extension of demand and an increase in demand. Describe in words how each appears on a graph.
scheme: B1: extension: more is bought because the good's own price falls
B1: on a graph, extension is a movement downward along the same demand curve
B1: increase: more is bought at the same price because of a change in another factor such as income or tastes
B1: on a graph, increase is a shift of the whole demand curve to the right

long.q: Give three exceptions to the law of demand.
scheme: B1: Giffen goods: some very cheap staple goods bought by the poor, of which more is bought when the price rises
B1: prestige (Veblen) goods such as diamonds, bought more when dearer because they show status
B1: expectation of a further rise in price, or emergencies such as war or famine, when people buy more even at higher prices

long.q: Individual demand: at ₹10, A buys 5 and B buys 3; at ₹8, A buys 7 and B buys 5; at ₹6, A buys 10 and B buys 8. Prepare the market demand schedule and state what it shows.
scheme: B1: at ₹10 market demand = 5 + 3 = 8 units
B1: at ₹8 it is 12 units and at ₹6 it is 18 units
B1: as the price falls, the quantity demanded rises: the law of demand (the market demand curve slopes downward)

long.q: Explain how a rise in the price of petrol may affect the demand for cars.
scheme: B1: cars and petrol are complementary goods, used together
B1: when petrol becomes dearer, running a car costs more, so the demand for cars falls (the demand curve for cars shifts to the left)

questions.q: According to the law of supply, other things being equal:
o: A rise in price raises the quantity supplied
A rise in price lowers the quantity supplied
Price has no effect on supply
questions.why: Higher prices make it more profitable to sell, so sellers offer more: a direct relationship.

questions.q: A farmer has 100 kg of wheat and offers 60 kg for sale at ₹25 a kilogram. His supply at that price is:
questions.why: Stock is the total quantity he has (100 kg); supply is the part offered for sale at a given price (60 kg).

questions.q: An improvement in technology that lowers the cost of production causes:
o: A shift of the supply curve to the left
A shift of the supply curve to the right (an increase in supply)
questions.why: With lower costs, firms can offer more at every price, so the whole supply curve shifts right.

questions.q: A new tax on the production of a good causes:
o: A decrease in supply (a leftward shift)
questions.why: The tax raises the cost of production, so less is offered at each price.

questions.q: The supply curve usually slopes upward from left to right because:
o: Higher prices give sellers a greater incentive to sell
Consumers buy more at higher prices
Costs always fall as output rises
questions.why: At higher prices more producers find it profitable to sell and existing ones offer more.

long.q: Distinguish between stock and supply.
scheme: B1: stock is the total quantity of a good that sellers have at a point of time
B1: supply is the quantity that sellers are willing to offer for sale at a given price and time; it can never exceed the stock

long.q: State four determinants of supply.
scheme: B1: the price of the good itself
B1: the prices (costs) of factors of production
B1: the state of technology
B1: government policy (taxes and subsidies), or prices of other goods, or the number of firms

long.q: Distinguish between a contraction of supply and a decrease in supply.
scheme: B1: contraction: less is supplied because the good's own price falls; it is a movement down along the same supply curve
B1: decrease: less is supplied at the same price because of a change in another factor, such as higher costs; the whole supply curve shifts to the left

long.q: Individual supply: at ₹5, firm X offers 10 units and firm Y offers 15; at ₹10, X offers 20 and Y 25; at ₹15, X offers 30 and Y 35. Prepare the market supply schedule.
scheme: B1: at ₹5, market supply = 10 + 15 = 25 units
B1: at ₹10 it is 45 units
B1: at ₹15 it is 65 units, showing that supply rises with price

long.q: State three exceptions to the law of supply.
scheme: B1: perishable goods such as vegetables, which must be sold even if prices fall
B1: sellers who expect prices to fall further, or who urgently need cash, sell more even at low prices
B1: agricultural output, which depends on weather and cannot be increased at once when prices rise (also accept: supply of labour at very high wages may fall)

questions.q: The demand for salt is usually:
questions.why: Salt is a necessity with few substitutes and takes a tiny part of income, so price changes hardly affect demand.

questions.q: A 10% fall in price leads to a 10% rise in the quantity demanded. Demand is:
questions.why: The percentage change in quantity equals the percentage change in price, so elasticity = 1.

questions.q: A good with many close substitutes has demand that is:
questions.why: If its price rises, buyers can easily switch to substitutes, so the quantity demanded falls sharply.

questions.q: A vertical demand curve shows:
questions.why: The same quantity is bought whatever the price, so elasticity is zero.

questions.q: In the very short run, the supply of perishable goods such as fish is:
questions.why: Such goods cannot be stored or produced quickly, so supply responds little to price in the short run.

long.q: Define price elasticity of demand and state the formula used in the percentage method.
scheme: B1: price elasticity of demand is the degree of responsiveness of the quantity demanded to a change in the good's price
B1: Ed = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price

long.q: Explain the five types of price elasticity of demand, describing in words the shape of the demand curve for each.
scheme: B1: perfectly elastic (Ed = ∞): a tiny price change causes an infinite change in demand; a horizontal straight line
B1: perfectly inelastic (Ed = 0): demand does not change with price; a vertical straight line
B1: unitary elastic (Ed = 1): the percentage change in demand equals that in price; a rectangular hyperbola
B1: relatively elastic (Ed > 1): demand changes by a larger percentage than price; a flatter curve
B1: relatively inelastic (Ed < 1): demand changes by a smaller percentage than price; a steeper curve

long.q: Explain four factors that determine the price elasticity of demand.
scheme: B1: nature of the good: necessities have inelastic demand, luxuries elastic demand
B1: availability of substitutes: more close substitutes make demand more elastic
B1: proportion of income spent: goods taking a small share of income (e.g. matchboxes) have inelastic demand
B1: number of uses, possibility of postponing purchase, habits, or the time period considered

long.q: Why is the demand for luxuries elastic while the demand for necessities is inelastic? Give an example of each.
scheme: B1: luxuries such as air conditioners can be postponed or given up, so buyers respond strongly to price changes
B1: necessities such as rice or salt must be bought whatever the price, so demand changes little

long.q: Explain three factors that affect the elasticity of supply.
scheme: B1: time period: supply is more elastic in the long run, when producers can adjust output and capacity
B1: nature of the good: perishable goods have inelastic supply; durable, storable goods more elastic supply
B1: cost of production and availability of inputs: if extra output raises costs sharply, supply is less elastic

questions.q: A firm under perfect competition is a:
questions.why: Each firm is too small to affect the market price, so it accepts the price set by industry demand and supply.

questions.q: Product differentiation and heavy advertising are features of:
questions.why: Many sellers sell similar but differentiated products (e.g. soaps, toothpastes) and spend on advertising.

questions.q: A single company that alone supplies electricity in a city, with no close substitute, is closest to:
questions.why: A monopoly has one seller of a product with no close substitutes and barriers to the entry of others.

questions.q: Interdependence among firms in fixing prices is the key feature of:
questions.why: With only a few sellers, each firm must consider how its rivals will react to its price changes.

questions.q: Charging different prices to different buyers for the same product is called:
questions.why: A monopolist can charge, for example, lower electricity rates to farmers than to factories.

long.q: State four features of perfect competition.
scheme: B1: a very large number of buyers and sellers
B1: homogeneous (identical) products
B1: free entry and exit of firms
B1: perfect knowledge of the market and a single uniform price

long.q: Explain three features of monopoly.
scheme: B1: a single seller controls the whole supply of the product
B1: there are no close substitutes for the product
B1: strong barriers prevent new firms from entering, so the monopolist is a price maker (and may practise price discrimination)

long.q: Distinguish between perfect competition and monopolistic competition (three points).
scheme: B1: products are identical under perfect competition but differentiated under monopolistic competition
B1: there are no selling costs under perfect competition, while advertising is heavy under monopolistic competition
B1: a firm under perfect competition is a price taker; under monopolistic competition it has some control over its price

long.q: Explain two features of oligopoly and give an example of an oligopolistic industry in India.
scheme: B1: a few large sellers produce most of the output
B1: firms are interdependent: each watches and reacts to its rivals' prices and advertising (also accept barriers to entry or price rigidity)
B1: example, e.g. mobile telephone services, cement or automobiles

long.q: What is meant by a market in economics? Why does it not need a physical place?
scheme: B1: a market is the whole area over which buyers and sellers of a product are in contact with each other and a single price tends to prevail
B1: buyers and sellers can deal by telephone, the Internet or through agents, so they need not meet at one place

questions.q: The main difficulty of the barter system is the lack of:
questions.why: Each trader must find someone who has what he wants and also wants what he has.

questions.q: Using money to repay a loan next year is its function as a:
questions.why: Money allows payments to be settled in the future, which makes borrowing and lending easy.

questions.q: Currency notes that are accepted because the government has declared them legal tender are:
questions.why: Fiat money has value because of the government's order, not because of the material it is made of.

questions.q: In India, the ₹1 note is issued by:
o: The Government of India (Ministry of Finance)
questions.why: All other notes are issued by the RBI, but the one-rupee note is issued by the Government of India.

questions.q: Which is the correct order in the evolution of money?
questions.why: Goods such as grain and cattle came first, then metal coins, then paper notes and finally bank and digital money.

long.q: Explain three difficulties of the barter system.
scheme: B1: lack of a double coincidence of wants
B1: lack of a common measure of value, so the rate of exchange between goods is hard to fix
B1: indivisibility of some goods (e.g. a cow) and difficulty in storing wealth or making deferred payments

long.q: State the primary and secondary functions of money.
scheme: B1: primary: medium of exchange
B1: primary: measure of value (unit of account)
B1: secondary: standard of deferred payment
B1: secondary: store of value and transfer of value

long.q: Distinguish between limited legal tender and unlimited legal tender.
scheme: B1: limited legal tender can be refused for payments above a certain amount, e.g. small coins
B1: unlimited legal tender must be accepted for payments of any amount, e.g. RBI currency notes

long.q: How did money remove the need for a double coincidence of wants? Give an example.
scheme: B1: money is generally accepted, so a seller can sell to anyone for money and use it to buy from anyone else; exchange splits into a sale and a purchase
B1: example: a potter in Khurja sells pots for money and uses the money to buy rice from any shop, without needing a rice farmer who wants pots

long.q: Trace the evolution of money through four stages.
scheme: B1: commodity money: goods such as cattle, grain or shells used as money
B1: metallic money: coins of gold, silver and later cheaper metals
B1: paper money: currency notes issued by the government or the central bank
B1: bank (credit) money and plastic or digital money: cheques, debit cards and UPI payments

questions.q: A current account is most suited to:
o: Businesses that make many payments every day
questions.why: It allows any number of deposits and withdrawals, though it usually pays no interest.

questions.q: A fixed deposit is:
o: Withdrawable by cheque at any time without loss
An account that earns no interest
Kept for a fixed period at a higher rate of interest
questions.why: Money is locked in for a set term, so the bank can pay a higher rate than on savings deposits.

questions.q: An overdraft allows a customer to:
o: Withdraw more than the balance in a current account, up to a limit
questions.why: The bank lets the customer overdraw the account and charges interest only on the amount overdrawn.

questions.q: The cash reserve ratio is 20% and the initial deposit is ₹5 000. What is the maximum total of deposits the banking system can create?
questions.why: Total deposits = initial deposit × 1/r = 5 000 × 1/0.20 = ₹25 000.

questions.q: Collecting cheques and paying insurance premiums for a customer are:
questions.why: In agency functions the bank acts as an agent of its customer.

long.q: Distinguish between savings deposits and fixed deposits (three points).
scheme: B1: withdrawals: savings deposits can be withdrawn at any time; fixed deposits only after the fixed period (or with a penalty)
B1: interest: savings deposits earn a lower rate; fixed deposits a higher rate
B1: purpose: savings deposits suit households' small savings and day-to-day needs; fixed deposits suit money not needed for a definite period

long.q: Explain credit creation by commercial banks, taking an initial deposit of ₹10 000 and a cash reserve ratio of 10%.
scheme: B1: the bank keeps 10% (₹1 000) as cash reserve and lends the remaining ₹9 000
B1: the borrower's spending comes back to banks as a new deposit, of which 90% is lent again; the process repeats
M1: total deposits = initial deposit × 1/r = 10 000 × 1/0.10
A1: = ₹1 00 000, so credit created = ₹90 000

long.q: State two agency functions and two general utility functions of a commercial bank.
scheme: B1: agency: collecting cheques and bills for customers
B1: agency: paying insurance premiums, bills or taxes on standing instructions (or buying and selling securities)
B1: utility: providing safe-deposit lockers
B1: utility: issuing bank drafts, letters of credit or traveller's cheques

long.q: Explain two ways in which commercial banks advance loans.
scheme: B1: cash credit or overdraft: the customer may draw up to an agreed limit and pays interest only on the amount used
B1: loans: a fixed sum is lent against security and repaid in instalments (also accept discounting bills of exchange)

long.q: Give two limitations on the power of commercial banks to create credit.
scheme: B1: the cash reserve ratio fixed by the RBI: the higher it is, the less banks can lend
B1: the habits of the public (holding more cash) and the availability of creditworthy borrowers and security

questions.q: The Reserve Bank of India was established in:
questions.why: The RBI began working on 1 April 1935 and was nationalised in 1949.

questions.q: To control inflation, the RBI would:
o: Buy government securities in the open market
questions.why: A higher bank rate makes borrowing dearer for banks and their customers, reducing credit and spending.

questions.q: The RBI acting as the 'lender of last resort' means that it:
o: Helps commercial banks facing a shortage of cash
questions.why: When a bank cannot get funds elsewhere, the RBI lends to it to prevent its collapse.

questions.q: Which is a qualitative (selective) method of credit control?
questions.why: Moral suasion uses persuasion and advice to direct credit; the others control the total volume of credit.

questions.q: The demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1 000 notes in India was announced on:
questions.why: On that date the old ₹500 and ₹1 000 notes ceased to be legal tender.

long.q: Explain four functions of the Reserve Bank of India.
scheme: B1: bank of issue: it has the sole right to issue currency notes (except the ₹1 note)
B1: banker to the government: it keeps government accounts and manages public debt
B1: bankers' bank and lender of last resort: it holds banks' reserves and lends to them in need
B1: controller of credit and custodian of foreign exchange reserves

long.q: Explain how the RBI uses the bank rate to control credit during inflation.
scheme: B1: the bank rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks (or rediscounts their bills)
B1: during inflation the RBI raises the bank rate, so banks borrow at a higher cost and raise their own lending rates
B1: borrowing becomes dearer, so credit, spending and the pressure on prices fall

long.q: Explain open market operations.
scheme: B1: open market operations are the buying and selling of government securities by the RBI in the open market
B1: selling securities takes cash out of banks and reduces credit (used in inflation); buying them adds cash and expands credit

long.q: Distinguish between the cash reserve ratio (CRR) and the statutory liquidity ratio (SLR).
scheme: B1: CRR is the percentage of a bank's deposits that it must keep as cash with the RBI
B1: SLR is the percentage of deposits that a bank must keep itself in liquid assets such as cash, gold or approved government securities

long.q: State three objectives of the demonetisation of 2016 and one difficulty it caused.
scheme: B1: to bring black money (unaccounted income) into the open
B1: to remove counterfeit (fake) currency notes
B1: to cut off funds for terrorism and to encourage digital payments
B1: difficulty, e.g. long queues at banks and a cash shortage that hurt small traders, farmers and daily-wage workers

questions.q: Which of these is a direct tax?
questions.why: The burden of income tax is borne by the person on whom it is levied; it cannot be shifted.

questions.q: Under a progressive tax, the rate of tax:
o: Is the same for all incomes
questions.why: Higher incomes pay a higher percentage, as in India's income-tax slabs.

questions.q: The Goods and Services Tax came into force in India on:
questions.why: GST replaced many indirect taxes of the Centre and the States from 1 July 2017.

questions.q: A fine paid for breaking a traffic rule is:
questions.why: Fines and penalties are sources of non-tax revenue; they are meant to prevent offences, not to raise income.

questions.q: Building a new dam is an example of:
questions.why: It creates a lasting asset, so it is capital expenditure.

long.q: Give two differences between direct and indirect taxes, and one example of each.
scheme: B1: the burden (incidence) of a direct tax falls on the person who pays it; an indirect tax can be shifted to others, e.g. buyers
B1: direct taxes are levied on income and property; indirect taxes on goods and services
B1: direct tax example: income tax or corporation tax
B1: indirect tax example: GST or customs duty

long.q: A person with an income of ₹1 00 000 pays ₹5 000 in tax, and a person with an income of ₹2 00 000 pays ₹20 000. Is the tax progressive, proportional or regressive? Show your working.
scheme: A1: the rate rises with income, so the tax is progressive

long.q: What is public debt? Distinguish between internal debt and external debt.
scheme: B1: public debt is the money borrowed by the government from the public, banks or other countries
B1: internal debt is borrowed from within the country and repaid in rupees
B1: external debt is borrowed from foreign governments or institutions such as the World Bank and must usually be repaid in foreign currency

long.q: Distinguish between revenue expenditure and capital expenditure, with an example of each.
scheme: B1: revenue expenditure creates no asset and is for the normal running of government
B1: capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities
B1: examples: salaries or interest payments (revenue); building roads, dams or schools (capital)

long.q: Explain four reasons for the growth of public expenditure in India.
scheme: B1: rising expenditure on defence and internal security
B1: growth of population and urbanisation, needing more public services
B1: the welfare state: more spending on education, health, subsidies and poverty programmes
B1: development of infrastructure, rising prices, and interest payments on public debt

questions.q: Inflation means:
o: A fall in the general price level
A sustained rise in the general price level
A rise in the price of one good
questions.why: Inflation is a continuing rise in prices in general, which means a fall in the value of money.

questions.q: During inflation, which group generally loses?
o: People with fixed incomes, such as pensioners
questions.why: Their money income stays the same while prices rise, so their real income falls.

questions.q: Inflation caused by rising wages and raw-material costs is:
questions.why: Higher costs push producers to raise prices even if demand has not risen.

questions.q: A very rapid, out-of-control rise in prices is called:
questions.why: In hyperinflation prices rise so fast that money loses its value and people lose faith in it.

questions.q: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures changes in:
o: Wholesale prices of goods traded between businesses
Retail prices of a basket of goods and services bought by consumers
questions.why: CPI tracks what households pay for items such as food, clothing, housing and transport.

long.q: Distinguish between demand-pull and cost-push inflation, giving two causes of each.
scheme: B1: demand-pull inflation occurs when total demand exceeds the available supply of goods
B1: causes, e.g. an increase in the money supply and a rise in incomes or government spending
B1: cost-push inflation occurs when rising costs of production push prices up
B1: causes, e.g. higher wages and a rise in the prices of raw materials or fuel

long.q: Explain the effect of inflation on debtors and creditors.
scheme: B1: debtors gain, because they repay loans in money that has lost purchasing power
B1: creditors lose, because the money they get back buys less than the money they lent

long.q: Describe the four stages of inflation.
scheme: B1: creeping inflation: prices rise very slowly and steadily; considered healthy for growth
B1: walking inflation: prices rise at a moderate but noticeable rate; a warning signal
B1: running inflation: prices rise rapidly and the value of money falls sharply
B1: hyperinflation: prices rise at an extremely fast, uncontrollable rate and money becomes almost worthless

long.q: Distinguish between the Wholesale Price Index and the Consumer Price Index. Why does a rise in the prices of the food basket hurt poor households most?
scheme: B1: WPI measures changes in the prices of goods at the wholesale (bulk) level between businesses; it does not include services
B1: CPI measures changes in the retail prices paid by consumers for goods and services
B1: poor households spend a large share of their income on food items such as cereals, pulses, milk and vegetables, so food inflation cuts their real income most

long.q: How does mild inflation affect production? Why is hyperinflation harmful to production?
scheme: B1: under mild inflation producers expect higher profits, so they invest and raise output and employment
B1: under hyperinflation costs and prices become unpredictable, so planning and investment stop
B1: people hoard goods and lose faith in money, savings fall, and resources move to speculation instead of production

questions.q: AGMARK is a quality certification mark for:
questions.why: AGMARK certifies the quality of farm products such as ghee, honey, pulses and spices.

questions.q: The ISI mark is granted by:
o: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
questions.why: BIS certifies that industrial products such as electrical appliances meet Indian standards.

questions.q: A shopkeeper mixes brick powder into chilli powder. This is:
questions.why: Adulteration is mixing cheaper or harmful substances into a product, lowering its quality.

questions.q: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the right to approach a consumer commission for compensation is the:
questions.why: The right to seek redressal lets a consumer get relief against unfair trade practices or defective goods.

questions.q: The Right to Information Act in India was passed in:
questions.why: The RTI Act, 2005 lets citizens obtain information from public authorities, including about public services.

long.q: State four ways in which consumers are exploited.
scheme: B1: underweight or short measurement
B1: adulteration and sale of substandard or duplicate goods
B1: charging more than the maximum retail price, or hoarding to raise prices
B1: false or misleading advertisements and poor after-sales service

long.q: Explain three rights of consumers under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
scheme: B1: right to safety: protection against goods and services dangerous to life and property
B1: right to be informed: about the quality, quantity, price, standard and expiry date of goods
B1: right to choose (or to be heard, to seek redressal, or to consumer awareness), correctly explained

long.q: State three duties of a consumer.
scheme: B1: buy goods with quality marks such as ISI, AGMARK or Hallmark
B1: always ask for a proper bill or cash memo and keep it
B1: read labels (price, expiry date) and file a complaint when cheated

long.q: What is food adulteration? State two of its harmful effects.
scheme: B1: food adulteration is mixing inferior, cheaper or harmful substances into food, or removing valuable parts, so that its quality falls
B1: it causes illness, such as stomach disorders, and can lead to serious diseases like cancer or paralysis
B1: consumers pay full price for inferior food and lose nutrition

long.q: Explain how the Public Distribution System and the ECOMARK protect consumers.
scheme: B1: the PDS supplies essential goods such as rice, wheat and sugar at subsidised prices through fair price (ration) shops
B1: it protects poor consumers from high prices, shortages and hoarding
B1: ECOMARK is a government label, administered through BIS, for products that cause little harm to the environment
B1: it helps consumers identify and choose eco-friendly products
